title: Crumpets with Butter
subtitle: Griddle-cooked yeast crumpets with spongy holes and a generous knob of butter
excerpt: Homemade crumpets made from a simple yeasted batter that produces the characteristic spongy, hole-filled texture when cooked in rings on a hot griddle. Served hot with enough butter to pool in every hole, the only correct approach.
sourceNotes: English crumpets appear in recipe literature from the mid-19th century. Mrs Beeton includes a recipe in Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136. The distinctive holey texture results from the interplay between yeast fermentation and bicarbonate of soda, which creates bubbles that rise through the batter as it sets.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cool completely before freezing. Toast from frozen, they come out exactly as good as freshly made.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the batch and freeze half. Crumpets are one of the best batchable breakfasts.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The batter can be made the night before up to the end of the first prove. Cover and refrigerate. The next morning, stir in the bicarbonate dissolved in a little warm water and leave for 20 minutes at room temperature before cooking.

glossaryTerms.definition: To allow the yeast batter to ferment and bubble before cooking, creating the gas bubbles that rise through the crumpet as it sets and form the characteristic holes.

content.text: Homemade crumpets are one of those things that reveal how much better a simple food can be when it's fresh. Shop-bought crumpets are reliable but slightly rubbery; crumpets cooked at home and eaten ten minutes later have a spongy, pillowy texture and a yeasty depth of flavour that is hard to replicate at scale. The process requires 7 g fast-action yeast, 200 ml warm water, 9 cm metal crumpet rings, and patience: the batter needs a full hour to
prove

before you cook. The holes, the defining feature, form when bubbles produced by the yeast rise through the batter and are set in place by the heat as the top surface dries. The bicarbonate of soda added after proving gives an extra boost of gas and ensures reliable holes even if the yeast is slightly sluggish.

items.prepNote: for serving, or more, to taste

content.text: Making the batter

Combine 200 ml warm water and the {{whole-milk}} milk in a jug, both should be comfortably warm, around 37°C. Stir in 7 g fast-action yeast and leave for five minutes. Tip the {{strong-bread-flour}} flour and {{sea-salt-flakes}} salt into a large bowl and make a well. Pour in the yeast mixture and whisk to a smooth, thick batter, like a thick pancake batter. Cover with a damp cloth and leave in a warm place to
prove
for 60 minutes. The batter should be visibly bubbly and have risen in the bowl.

Dissolve the {{bicarbonate-of-soda}} bicarbonate of soda in 1 tablespoon of warm water and stir into the proved batter. Leave for a further 20 minutes. The batter will bubble again as the bicarbonate reacts with the acids produced during fermentation. Don't skip this step, it's what ensures you get the characteristic grid of holes.
Cooking the crumpets

Set the frying pan over a medium-low heat. Lightly grease the inside of each 9 cm metal crumpet ring with a small amount of butter or neutral oil. Place the rings in the pan and leave for a minute to get hot. Pour or ladle the batter into each ring to about 1.5 cm deep, the batter should spread to fill the ring without spilling over. You may find you can cook two or three at a time depending on pan size.

Cook without moving for 5 to 7 minutes. Watch the surface: holes will begin to appear within the first minute, and by the time the crumpet is ready the surface should be covered in bubbles that have opened and dried, giving a dimpled, matte appearance. The crumpet is ready to flip when the top no longer looks wet and the sides are set. Carefully lift off the ring, it should come away cleanly, and flip the crumpet for one final minute to set the top surface. The top should be just pale gold; the base should be deep honey-brown.
Serving

Eat immediately, with {{salted-butter}} butter pressed into every hole. The butter should melt fully, this requires the crumpet to be hot enough that it pools rather than just softens. Salted butter is traditional and correct. Honey or golden syrup can go over the top, but the butter must come first.
Where this dish lives

Crumpets belong to a specific corner of British food culture: the afternoon tea table and the winter weekend morning, eaten by the fire with a pot of strong tea. Mrs Beeton documented the recipe in 1861, and the basic method has barely changed since. They're sold in every supermarket but are noticeably better made at home, especially eaten still warm rather than toasted. The griddle-cooked surface and the yeasty batter are closer to what a muffin was before the American bakery tradition took the word.
Troubleshooter
No holes appearing:

Either the batter didn't prove long enough, the yeast wasn't active, or the heat is too high and the surface is setting before the bubbles can rise and open. Check the yeast by proofing it separately in warm water with a pinch of sugar, it should foam within ten minutes. Reduce the heat and allow more time.
Batter is leaking under the rings:

The batter is too thin or the rings aren't flat on the pan. Thicken the batter slightly by leaving it to rest another 20 minutes, the flour will absorb more liquid. Alternatively, press the rings down firmly before pouring.
Rings are sticking and tearing the crumpet:
Grease the inside of the rings more thoroughly. Crumpet batter is sticky and will adhere to any ungreased surface.
